result: The authors generated epidermal cell-specific PIEZO1 knockout mice (PIEZO1cKO) by crossing Krt14Cre and Piezo1loxp/loxp mice. Successful knockout was confirmed by RNAscope showing absence of Piezo1 puncta in PIEZO1cKO epidermis and qRT-PCR showing no Piezo1 transcript. PIEZO1 deletion did not disrupt gross epidermal morphology, and no sex differences were observed.
evaluation: Claims C26-31 provide converging evidence from multiple validation methods (RNAscope, qRT-PCR, H&E staining) confirming successful and specific knockout without gross morphological defects. The genetic approach is standard and well-documented (C135), and appropriate controls were used (C136).

result: Keratinocytes from wild-type mice and humans respond robustly to the PIEZO1-specific agonist Yoda1 in a concentration-dependent manner, while PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes are virtually unresponsive. This demonstrates that functional PIEZO1 is expressed in both mouse and human keratinocytes.
evaluation: Claims C32-36 show clear calcium imaging data demonstrating Yoda1 responses in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes, confirming specificity. The concentration-dependence (C32) and cross-species validation in human cells (C35, C115-116) strengthen the conclusion. The high percentage of responding cells (C137-138) supports widespread PIEZO1 expression.

result: PIEZO1 is critical for setting the mechanical threshold of keratinocytes. PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes required greater indentation to elicit mechanically activated currents and showed increased numbers of mechanically insensitive cells (51.35% vs 21.74% in wild-type). However, PIEZO1 deletion did not affect the proportion of rapidly, intermediately, or slowly adapting currents, nor the maximum current amplitude.
evaluation: Claims C37-45 present patch clamp data showing elevated mechanical thresholds (C39-40) and increased mechanically insensitive cells (C41, C91) in PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes. The lack of effect on current kinetics (C42) and amplitude (C43) suggests PIEZO1 specifically affects threshold rather than response magnitude. Sample sizes appear adequate (23-37 cells from n=5 mice per group).

result: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion selectively decreased the firing frequency of Aδ fibers during mechanical stimulation, particularly at higher forces (100-150mN), while having no effect on Aβ or C fiber firing. Mechanical thresholds were unchanged for all fiber types.
evaluation: Claims C47-52 show ex vivo tibial nerve recordings demonstrating fiber-type specific effects. The selective effect on Aδ fibers (C47, C97) at high forces (C48, C98) is well-documented, while the lack of effect on Aβ (C49, C100) and C fibers (C50, C103-104) is clearly stated. The unchanged thresholds (C51) suggest PIEZO1 affects response magnitude rather than detection threshold. Sample sizes are adequate (30-34 fibers from 17-19 mice).

result: Intraplantar injection of Yoda1 induced dose-dependent paw attending behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice. Yoda1 did not directly induce sensory fiber firing but increased mechanically-induced firing frequency of C fibers in wild-type preparations, an effect absent in PIEZO1cKO tissue. Yoda1 also sensitized wild-type mice to mechanical stimulation 30 minutes post-injection.
evaluation: Claims C53-64 demonstrate that Yoda1 acts through epidermal PIEZO1 to induce behavioral responses (C53-55, C120-122) via mechanical sensitization rather than direct neural activation (C56). The C fiber sensitization (C57, C60-61) and behavioral mechanical hypersensitivity (C62-63) provide mechanistic insight. The genotype-specific effects support PIEZO1 dependence.

result: PIEZO1cKO mice exhibited decreased behavioral responses to innocuous (von Frey filaments, paintbrush) and noxious (needle) mechanical stimuli, with the most pronounced deficits in needle responses. Heat and cold responses were normal, indicating specificity to mechanical modalities.
evaluation: Claims C65-73 present comprehensive behavioral data across multiple mechanical stimuli showing consistent deficits in PIEZO1cKO mice. The preserved thermal responses (C68-70) demonstrate specificity and rule out general somatosensory deficits. High-speed imaging (C71-73) provides quantitative measures of reflexive and affective behaviors. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=10-12 mice per group).

result: PIEZO1 is a key keratinocyte mechanotransducer that is critical for normal touch sensation in mice. This is the first demonstration of a role for PIEZO1 in tactile sensation. PIEZO1 is also expressed and functional in human keratinocytes.
evaluation: Claims C2, C74-75, C133-134 represent the main conclusions synthesized from all experimental results. The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from calcium imaging (functional expression), patch clamp (mechanotransduction), nerve recordings (neural signaling), and behavioral assays (touch sensation). The novelty claim (C75) appears justified as prior work focused on PIEZO2 in touch and PIEZO1 in other tissues. Human keratinocyte data (C134) extends translational relevance.
